newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik foes meet for peace talks in Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Tajik foes meet for peace talks in Afghanistan.

text.p: Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov met Islamist rebel leader Sayid Abdullo Nuri in northern Afghanistan for peace talks as further violence rocked the former Soviet republic.
Russia's Interfax news agency said negotiations were underway behind closed doors in northern Afghanistan.

Otakhon Latifi, an aide to Nuri quoted by Interfax, said the talks were to prepare the ground for a further meeting in Moscow later this month in which a ceasefire and some form of coalition government might be agreed.
However, previous ceasefire accords brokered by the United Nations have been regularly ignored and diplomats based in Dushanbe expect little from the negotiations.
On the eve of Rakhmonov's departure for Afghanistan, a gun battle between government troops and opposition fighters near Dushanbe left two dead.

"We carried out a raid on a suspected opposition base in Dzhangalabad when the shooting occurred," said a Tajik interior ministry spokesman, who said one government soldier was killed and another wounded in the attack.
A guerrilla comander was also killed in the raid and three opposition fighters were captured, he added.
Fighting has flared in Tajikistan since the peace talks were announced at the end of last month, with each side trying to beef up its position at the negotiating table.
The opposition are also widely blamed for a series of attacks against Russian servicemen based in Tajikistan who help shore up Rakhmonov's shaky administration.
The talks were delayed by a day after the U.N. aircraft in which Nuri was travelling to the meeting was forced to land by warplanes belonging to Afghanistan's purist Islamic Taleban militia.
The Taleban said on Sunday the aircraft had been released. U.N. spokeswoman Sylvana Foa said there was an apparent misunderstanding between the United Nations and the Taleban.

The four-year civil war has left tens of thousands dead and many more homeless in the remote, mountainous country bordering Afghanistan and China. Regional and clan rivalries underlie the conflict between the Islamist rebels and the secular government.
